title: The Goose and the Golden Egg

sentences.text: A farmer kept a goose that laid one golden egg each morning.
The egg shone in the straw, and the farmer sold it at the market for a good price.
At first the farmer was delighted. One egg a day was a steady treasure.
Then the farmer began to want that treasure all at once.
If the goose can make gold, the farmer said, there must be a heap of it somewhere.
The farmer searched the nest, the shed, and the yard, and found no hidden pile.
Impatient, the farmer tried to hurry the goose and take more than the one egg.
The goose flapped, slipped free, and flew to a far field.
The next morning the nest was empty. The morning after that, it was empty too.
The farmer still had the money from eggs already sold, but the daily gift was gone.
Wanting everything at once had cost the farmer the good thing that was already there.

questions.prompt: What is this story mostly about?

choices.text: Wanting everything at once and losing a daily gift
A market that stops selling ordinary eggs
A goose who learns to build a shed
A farmer who finds a heap of gold in the yard

questions.explanation: The goose already gives one golden egg a day. The farmer tries to take more, the goose leaves, and the nest stays empty. Greed is the main idea.

questions.prompt: The farmer grows impatient. What does impatient mean?

choices.text: Happy with one egg a day

questions.explanation: Impatient means not willing to wait. The farmer wants the treasure all at once instead of accepting one egg each morning.

questions.prompt: How many golden eggs does the goose lay each morning at the start?
questions.explanation: The opening line says the goose laid one golden egg each morning. The trouble starts when the farmer wants more than that.

choices.text: The market closed and eggs had no price
The nest was moved to the far field on purpose
The goose forgot how to lay an egg
The farmer would not wait and tried to take more than the daily egg

questions.explanation: The story does not say the goose is lost. It leaves right after the farmer tries to hurry it and take more. That pressure is the clue.

attribution: Inspired by a public-domain fable by Aesop. The wording is original, and the ending is gentler than the older version.
